narrativeReportMd:
# Linkage R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`Linkage` appears to have been removed from the R6 ballot core package with no direct in-package successor found. This is a hard R4-to-R6 instance break: an R4 resource with `resourceType: Linkage` has no R6 StructureDefinition to validate against and is likely to be rejected or treated as unknown by R6-only parsers, schemas, generated models, and APIs.

## Scope
The report is scoped to Linkage's local resource identity and local content model. Base `Resource`, `DomainResource`, `Element`, and `BackboneElement` changes are excluded. Search parameters and implementation-guide-specific migration policy are noted only as follow-up work.

## Main migration themes
The primary migration theme is retirement rather than field-level reshaping. R4 systems used Linkage to assert that multiple resource instances represented the same underlying occurrence and to label each linked resource as `source`, `alternate`, or `historical`. R6 core provides no equivalent Linkage resource in the supplied package, so migration requires a policy decision: retain legacy R4 Linkage records out of band, map them into a local extension/profile, or replace them with domain-specific relationships where those are clinically and operationally safe.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact finding is the missing R6 artifact itself. A second high-impact concern is semantic loss: the old `active`, `author`, and repeating `item` model has no standard R6 destination. The LinkageType terminology is also absent from the R6 core package, which affects enum generation and preservation of role semantics during custom migration.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is needed to decide whether each Linkage assertion should be retained, ignored, transformed to a local extension, or replaced by resource-specific relationships. The supplied computable definitions establish absence from the package but do not provide official rationale or an endorsed successor.

## Backward-compatible design observations
A less disruptive R6 design could have kept Linkage as a deprecated or retained trial-use resource, or could have published a replacement profile/extension plus ConceptMap. That would preserve validation and migration paths but would keep a low-maturity artifact in the core package.

## Follow-up analysis
Review cross-version migration guidance, any official R6 narrative page/change notes, Linkage search-parameter removal, and terminology carry-forward for `linkage-type` before choosing a production migration strategy.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `Linkage` is present in R4 but absent from the supplied R6 ballot core package, so R4 Linkage instances are not valid R6 core resources. The main migration concerns are resource-type rejection, loss of the arbitrary-resource linkage content model, and preserving the `source`/`alternate`/`historical` role semantics. Confidence is high for absence from the package and medium for replacement assessment because official diff/narrative migration notes were not supplied.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is not a simple element transform. Systems need to inventory existing R4 Linkage instances, decide whether the assertion still has business value, and choose a representation outside R6 core if it must be preserved. Options include retaining the original R4 resource in an archival store, using a local R6 extension/profile with explicit governance, or mapping individual relationships to domain-specific links where a resource-specific relationship has the same meaning. None of these is automatically lossless for all Linkage uses.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high that `Linkage` is absent from the supplied R6 package: the assigned file is missing, the R6 index has no StructureDefinition entry for Linkage, no R6 `*linkage*.json` files were found, and exact `Linkage` resource/type searches did not identify a successor. Confidence is lower for the reason and best migration path because the local inputs do not include official diff text, narrative pages, Jira history, or a cross-version ConceptMap.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation and runtime break. A syntactically valid R4 instance with `resourceType: Linkage` has no R6 core StructureDefinition, so an R6 validator or generated resource factory cannot validate or instantiate it as a known R6 resource. R6-to-R4 representability is not the main issue because there is no R6 Linkage content model to map back.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Linkage was low-maturity and likely uncommon, but where used it can affect record reconciliation, duplicate resolution, and source-of-truth decisions. Dropping it without review can change which record downstream systems treat as current.

justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain Linkage in R6 core as a deprecated or retired compatibility resource while discouraging new use.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of retiring a very low-maturity broad linkage resource is reasonable: R4 `Linkage` was trial-use/FMM 0, and the R6 package contains no `Linkage` StructureDefinition. The break is severe and the local inputs do not include the official rationale, so the removal is not conclusively justified. However, the true less-breaking base alternative would materially undercut the cleanup by keeping the old resource identity in R6 core, so the breaking design is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would have kept the same `resourceType: Linkage` and R4 element shape in R6 with a deprecated or retired status and clear guidance not to use it for new content. That is a real base-design alternative, unlike an external profile, local extension, or conversion script. It is only partial because R6 implementations would still need validators, parsers, generated classes, endpoints, and conformance metadata for a low-maturity arbitrary-resource equivalence model that may never disappear.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances and generated surfaces, but keeps a trial-use/FMM 0 arbitrary-resource linkage model in core and may require indefinite validator/API support.

findings.narrativeMd: `Linkage` has moved from being a concrete R4 resource to having no supplied R6 core StructureDefinition. This is not merely a renamed element or changed cardinality; the whole resource identity disappears. Implementers with generic FHIR parsers, generated model classes, JSON Schema/OpenAPI artifacts, or API routing keyed by resource type should expect `resourceType: Linkage` to become unknown in an R6-only stack.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid Linkage instance can become R6-invalid solely because the resource type is no longer defined. This affects validation, parsing, code generation, resource registries, REST endpoint availability, and bundle/resource-type dispatch. There is no R6-to-R4 loss for Linkage itself because R6 core does not define new Linkage instances.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory existing Linkage records before upgrade. Decide whether to archive them as R4 resources, expose them through a compatibility layer, transform them into a governed local extension/profile, or replace them with resource-specific relationships. Test R6 validators and parsers explicitly with historical Bundles containing `Linkage` resources, because failure mode may vary between rejection, unknown-resource preservation, or data loss.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The backward-compatible alternative would have been to retain Linkage in R6, possibly marked deprecated/retired, so old data could still validate and round-trip. That alternative would reduce migration breakage but keep a low-maturity resource in the core package. Without official rationale, the necessity of complete removal cannot be confirmed from local inputs alone.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm against official R6 narrative/change notes before making production policy. A successor might exist outside the supplied core package or as non-core guidance, but no direct local counterpart was found.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 defines `Linkage` as a concrete resource, while the supplied R6 package has no `StructureDefinition-Linkage.json` and no package-index entry for the resource. That makes a valid R4 `resourceType: Linkage` instance unknown to an R6-only validator, parser, generated model, or resource-type route. This is a real top-level compatibility break. However, the artifact was trial-use/FMM 0 in R4, so the removal does not carry a strong stability expectation by itself. A quick public-use check found some implementation relevance, including public GitHub matches and a Microsoft FHIR-Converter template, but no clear official production IG dependency in the quick search. Given the low maturity and the likely R6 goal of removing a broad, low-maturity arbitrary-resource linkage model, the break looks proportionate.

freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use substantially softens the stability concern. The break is hard, but low maturity means it should not be escalated solely because old instances become invalid; the limited public-use evidence prevents treating impact as zero.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: an R4 instance with resourceType Linkage has no R6 core StructureDefinition, so R6-only validation and resource factories cannot treat it as a known core resource.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking R6 base design could have retained Linkage as deprecated or retired. That would preserve R4 wire compatibility, but it would also keep generated classes, validator metadata, and possible API/search expectations for an FMM 0 arbitrary-resource linkage model. That tradeoff makes the alternative only partial, not an obvious low-cost requirement.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing report that this is a hard, high-confidence R4-to-R6 break and that a deprecated-retention alternative exists only partially; the fresh judgment gives more explicit weight to FMM 0.

justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have kept `Linkage.active`, `Linkage.author`, `Linkage.item`, `Linkage.item.type`, and `Linkage.item.resource` on a deprecated R6 `Linkage` resource. examples.examplesMd: The migration example is deliberately illustrative, not a recommended standard URL. It shows that preserving old semantics in R6 requires a governed local extension or other non-core representation.

findings.narrativeMd: Removing Linkage also removes its local assertion model. The important data is not just the list of references; it includes who asserted the linkage, whether it remains active, and which member is considered source, alternate, or historical. A naive migration that drops Linkage or maps only references loses these semantics.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: The old resource is invalid in R6 because the resource type is absent. If an implementation tries to transform the content, there is no standard R6 path that validators can check for the old `lnk-1` rule or for the required relationship between item role and target resource. This is therefore both a validation break and a conformance/semantic migration risk.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not automatically discard Linkage records. Classify existing records by target resource type and business purpose. For each class, decide whether a domain-specific R6 relationship is semantically equivalent; if not, preserve the assertion in an archival R4 store or a local R6 extension/profile with explicit definitions for `active`, `author`, role, and target reference. Include tests for inactive linkages, multiple alternate records, and historical records.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible approach could have preserved the model as a deprecated resource or provided a standard extension and transform. Complete removal may simplify the core specification, but it pushes migration design to implementers and increases the chance of incompatible local representations.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: This finding intentionally does not claim that any specific R6 resource is an adequate replacement. The local search found only unrelated uses of the word linkage or source-of-truth concepts.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The R4 `Linkage` content model includes `active`, `author`, and repeating `item` entries, with each item requiring a role and a reference to any FHIR Resource. R6 has no standard Linkage destination, so preserving those assertions in an R6-only system requires a local model or a domain-specific reinterpretation. That can be lossy, especially for source-of-truth and historical-record semantics. Still, this finding is largely the direct consequence of the resource removal rather than a separate mature element change. Because the R4 resource was FMM 0/trial-use and no quick official production dependency was found, carrying the whole arbitrary-resource assertion model forward in base R6 does not appear clearly required.

R4 Linkage.author: optional Reference to Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Organization responsible for asserting the linkage.

R4 Linkage.item.resource: required Reference to Resource, allowing arbitrary-resource linkage.

R6 package and index searches found no Linkage StructureDefinition or direct arbitrary-resource replacement; R6 Patient.link exists but only links Patient/RelatedPerson and does not carry the same general model.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use softens the concern even though migration can require judgment. The domain can matter for record reconciliation, but the low maturity and lack of clear official production-use evidence argue against treating this as disproportionate on its own.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: R6 generated models and APIs have no standard fields corresponding to Linkage.active, Linkage.author, Linkage.item.type, or Linkage.item.resource, so migration must use local or domain-specific representations.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: The main less-breaking base design is to retain the R4 Linkage content model inside a deprecated R6 Linkage resource. Patient.link or other resource-specific links may cover some patient identity cases but do not preserve arbitrary-resource sets, author, active status, or the old role semantics. Retaining Linkage would avoid data loss but would continue a broad FMM 0 model and duplicate more specific relationship mechanisms.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing report that the migration risk is real and that the less-breaking alternative is partial. The fresh review treats the finding as downstream of resource removal and therefore probably acceptable under FMM 0.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Removing terminology used only by a removed resource is understandable, but the R4 LinkageType system is small and self-contained. Keeping it as retired terminology would not require restoring the `Linkage` resource, endpoint, or content model, and would still support compatibility layers and historical validation. On the local evidence, the terminology removal appears more avoidable than the resource removal itself.

This is a base-package alternative, not merely conversion tooling. It would let validators, generators, extensions, and migration guides continue to refer to the canonical R4 role codes `source`, `alternate`, and `historical`.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Low to moderate tradeoff: a small dormant legacy terminology remains visible, but terminology resolution and enum generation for preserved Linkage data continue to work.

findings.narrativeMd: The role code is central to Linkage semantics. Without preserving `source`, `alternate`, or `historical`, a migrated assertion may still show that two resources are related but lose which record should be preferred or treated as obsolete.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 validation required one of the LinkageType codes for every item. R6 core validation has no Linkage element or binding, so the old code field is not directly valid. If a migration uses an extension, validators will need the R4 terminology package or a local terminology definition to validate the preserved codes.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Carry the three role codes explicitly in any custom migration model and document their original R4 definitions. If using a local extension, bind it to a retained copy of `http://hl7.org/fhir/linkage-type` or to a well-documented local code system with a ConceptMap from the R4 codes. Test all three roles, especially `historical`, because it can affect whether downstream systems continue to update a record.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Retaining the terminology as historical would have avoided enum and terminology-resolution churn even if the resource was retired. Because the supplied R6 package removes both the resource and the local terminology artifacts, migration tooling must supply its own terminology context.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 required `Linkage.item.type` to use the LinkageType value set, with the small code system `source`, `alternate`, and `historical`. R6 no longer includes the Linkage resource and also omits the LinkageType CodeSystem and ValueSet from the core package. Unlike restoring the whole resource, retaining retired or historical terminology would be a narrow compatibility measure: it would help validators, generated enums, extensions, and migration tooling preserve the meaning of legacy Linkage records without requiring an R6 Linkage endpoint or content model. Because the codes distinguish source-of-truth from alternate or obsolete records, dropping the canonical terminology seems more avoidable than the resource removal itself.

The Linkage-local `lnk-1` invariant was checked and is discussed in the content-model finding. No separate surviving R6 constraint comparison is possible without a counterpart artifact.
